## Overview

The phrase "West is best" is a staple of NBA discourse — but does the data back it up at the division level? Building on their basketball analytics episodes, Jess and Rich aggregate team performance across divisions and conferences, comparing strength using win percentage and related metrics. The episode explains how the NBA's geographic structure shapes playoff narratives and whether simple league tables tell the full story.

## Key Concepts

::: {.callout-tip}
## NBA Conference and Division Structure
The NBA splits teams into Eastern and Western conferences, each with three divisions. Playoff seeding is conference-based, so cross-conference strength debates often matter for predicting finals matchups rather than regular-season titles alone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Win Percentage as a Comparison Tool
Because basketball games do not end in draws, win percentage provides a direct way to compare teams and aggregate division strength — though uneven schedules complicate head-to-head conclusions.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Aggregating Team Strength to Divisions
Ranking divisions requires deciding how to weight teams (mean win percentage, median, top-heavy vs depth). Different choices can shift the story the data tells.
:::

## Transcript Highlights

> "Everyone says the West is tougher — we wanted to see if that's true when you actually line the divisions up."

The episode frames a popular talking point as a testable statistical question.

***

> "Divisions are a bit arbitrary geographically, but they're how the league organises the schedule and the narrative."

Rich notes that analytical choices should respect how the NBA structures competition even when divisions are not the only meaningful unit.

## Discussion

This episode bridges explainer content on NBA structure and applied ranking analysis. It pairs naturally with the Elo-based playoff prediction in Episode 14: understanding conference and division strength provides context for why certain seeds and matchups surprise fans each spring. The hosts emphasise that a single aggregate statistic rarely settles debate — but transparent ranking methods make disagreement more productive.
